summary: Reports on a workshop held in February 1994 at USC's Information Sciences Institute, initiated by the IAB, that focused on security issues in the Internet architecture. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts met to talk about keeping the Internet safe, and this note writes down what they discussed.

subtitle: Workshop report on security challenges as the Internet adds new services.

tldr.problem: As the Internet moved beyond best-effort datagram delivery to support quality-of-service, mobility, multicast, and routing, new security threats emerged that existing point-to-point security techniques could not fully address.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB workshop brought together 30 experts to identify four top-level security requirements: end-to-end security, end-system security (firewalls), secure quality-of-service, and secure network infrastructure. The group developed architectural approaches to each.
tldr.outcome: The workshop produced recommendations for immediate actions (site security, one-time passwords, firewall guidelines) and longer-term research directions, establishing a foundation for security work in emerging Internet services.

today: RFC 1636 is an Informational RFC documenting the IAB's early analysis of security in the emerging Internet. The workshop's identification of secure QOS, firewall architectures, and authentication infrastructure as key areas proved prescient; these areas became major research and standardization topics in subsequent years. The report's long-term recommendations remain relevant as the Internet continues to evolve.

sections.title: Why the IAB Held This Workshop
sections.content:
By early 1994, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and Internet Architecture Board (IAB) recognized that security and scaling were the two most important problems facing the Internet. While scaling (the IPv4 address crisis) had spawned the IPng effort, security had received less organized attention. In February 1994, the IAB held a workshop at USC's Information Sciences Institute to explore how security should be integrated with other Internet architecture issues.

The workshop deliberately focused on long-term architectural questions rather than quick tactical fixes. Attendees included IAB members, IETF area directors, and experts in routing, mobility, realtime service, and security. The ground rule: valid discussion topics had to involve both security and at least one other area (routing, mobility, or realtime service). The 30 participants were divided into three breakout groups, each with representation from all specialties, to identify interconnections between security and these emerging capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB said, 'Security is important, but the Internet is changing. We need to think about how to keep it safe when people use it for video, phone calls, and other new things.'

sections.title: Four Key Security Requirements
sections.content:
The workshop identified four top-level security requirements. End-to-end security ensures confidentiality, authentication, and integrity for communications between endpoints. Existing techniques (symmetric encryption, message digests, key management) are well-suited for point-to-point applications, though the workshop noted that for export reasons, separating authentication from privacy might be wise.

End-system security recognizes that firewalls are a practical necessity for large organizations. Two models were discussed: application-layer firewalls (relays) and IP-layer firewalls (filters). Secure quality-of-service (QOS) addresses a new problem: when the network offers special treatment to some packets (low latency, high bandwidth), attackers could steal those resources or deny service. Secure network infrastructure protects routers and DNS servers from attacks that could disrupt operations or spread false routing information.

A particularly contentious issue emerged around certificate naming: should the Internet use DNS domain names (simple, familiar, but 'weak') or X.509 distinguished names (more powerful, but complex and lacking deployment infrastructure)? The group could not reach consensus, deferring the question to the broader community.
sections.plainLanguage: The group said security needs to handle four things: protecting messages end-to-end, protecting organizations from outside attacks, making sure special network treatment can't be stolen, and protecting routers and name servers.

sections.title: Firewall Architecture
sections.content:
The workshop spent considerable time on firewall design. Application-layer firewalls operate as relays: a client connects to the firewall instead of the server, the firewall verifies authentication and authorization, then relays traffic. Advantage: the firewall sees all application data and can reject malformed requests. Disadvantages: requires application-specific code for each protocol, becomes a single point of failure, and can hurt performance.

IP-layer firewalls filter packets based on header information (addresses, ports, protocol). They are transparent to applications and general-purpose. The workshop proposed a detailed mechanism: when a client's packet doesn't match any rule, the firewall returns an 'Authentication Required' error, listing trusted authentication servers. The client authenticates with one of those servers, requests authorization for its intended access, and the firewall rule is updated to allow the traffic. To prevent spoofing of source addresses, three techniques were identified: checking only the packet profile (weak), sealing packets with a shared secret, or signing packets with public keys. Each approach trades off security against computational cost.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall is like a bouncer at a club. It can check ID at the door (IP firewall) or walk with each guest to each room (application firewall). Either way, you have to prove who you are.

sections.title: Secure Quality-of-Service Forwarding
sections.content:
Quality-of-service (QOS) allows the network to treat some packet flows preferentially. But if users can claim QOS without authorization, they steal resources or cause denial-of-service. The workshop developed a two-stage model: setup stage, where a user requests and proves entitlement to a service class, and classification stage, where routers recognize packets belonging to that class.

Setup involves high-level credentials (HLID). Classification requires each packet to carry a low-level identifier (LLID) plus an authenticator proving the packet belongs to the authorized class. The LLID must be independent of the packet's addresses, so user privileges don't change if their IP address changes (important for mobile users). Three techniques for validating LLIDs were discussed: digital signatures (slow but strong), sealing with a shared secret (fast but requires trusting all routers with the secret), and temporary passwords (very fast but weak). The appropriate technique depends on performance requirements and threat model. LLIDs should be short-lived, and routers can validate selectively rather than every packet, for performance.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want special treatment (like a video call), you ask the network and prove you deserve it (setup). Then every packet you send carries a ticket showing you paid for that service (LLID).

sections.title: Authentication and Credentials
sections.content:
As security becomes distributed across the Internet, a common authentication infrastructure is needed. The workshop identified two approaches: identity-based authorization, where a user has multiple identities (like holding different credit cards) representing different roles or affiliations, and capability-based authorization, where a user has few identities but carries signed credentials delegating specific permissions.

For multicast (group communication), symmetric encryption provides confidentiality for the group, but authenticating individual sources is computationally expensive and requires careful key management. The workshop noted that plug-and-play security is essential: when a device joins a network, it must authenticate before accessing services, but this must work at scale without manual configuration. A short-term approach to password protection, proposed by one group, was encryption at the TCP connection level, allowing one-time keys to be exchanged during the connection handshake, though patent and export control issues were noted.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a way to prove who you are that works everywhere on the Internet. For group video calls, everyone shares a key so eavesdroppers can't listen in.

sections.title: Recommendations for Action
sections.content:
Short-term actions focused on immediate defense: run security probes to find weak passwords (using tools like CRACK, ISS, SATAN), establish channels for publishing security risk information, deploy one-time password systems (S/Key, SecurID), update the Site Security Handbook, and encourage Kerberos deployment. Guidelines for protocol developers and firewall-friendly applications were recommended.

Medium-term actions required protocol design and engineering: develop an Internet-wide authentication protocol, improve Kerberos to work with public-key systems, push PEM/RIPEM/PGP email security, develop authenticated DNS, establish certificate server infrastructure, and engineer authentication for the Web.

Long-term research addressed harder problems: controlling executable code, countering router sabotage, preventing Byzantine routing attacks, proxy computing, and the role of viruses. The workshop cautioned that security must be added incrementally, as a scheme requiring simultaneous changes to applications, DNS, routers, and firewalls would be too hard to deploy.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, use tools to find bad passwords and teach people to use one-time codes. Soon, build a global way to verify who you are. Long-term, figure out how to stop hackers from breaking routers and sending fake routing information.
